newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Exports high but market slow.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Exports high but market slow.

text.p: Australia's grains market continued to firm in slow trading last week while huge tonnages of wheat exports poured funds into the country's international account.

Preliminary figures from the Australian Wheat Board show that Australia exported 2.1 million to 2.2 million tonnes of wheat in January, taking the total to 5.3 million tonnes so far in the shipping year, from October 1 to end-January.
This "creamed" last year's exports, Alex Nichol of the Australian Wheat Board commented on Friday.
Australia exported 1.4 million tonnes of wheat in January 1995, while exports for the period from October 1 to end-January amounted to 3.1 million tonnes.
Wheat exports produce an immediate flow of funds into Australia's current account, with most exports paid for by letter of credit at the time of shipment.
For exports to Iraq under the United Nations food-for-oil deal, Australia requires lodgement of funds in escrow in advance of shipment.

AWB sources and finance sector analysts said on Friday that wheat sales were a major factor behind Australia's eight percent rise in December exports, which cut the country's current account deficit by more than the market expected.
While shipments continue to ride high, last week was quiet in both domestic and international sales.
This was despite a firming in Australian domestic prices and further negotiations by the AWB for further export deals.
Australia was after wheat sales to India and Egypt, but no news was yet to hand, the AWB's Nichol said on Friday.
After its unusual sale of one million tonnes of wheat to usually self-sufficient India in December, AWB last week pursued a smaller Indian requirement for a reported 50,000 tonnes.
AWB also attempted to strike further wheat deals with Egypt, which the trade says is seeking 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes.
Australia's domestic market was slow, choppy and frustrating, according to Guy Allen of NSW grain handling and trading co-operative GrainCorp.
Cash grain bids and offers were wide apart in little activity. Farmers were tight holders, end-users need to buy grain but were yet to do so, he said.
Prices changed only slightly, with the weaker Australian dollar underpinning the domestic market, he said.
Allen saw the price of Australian Standard White (ASW) wheat delivered Newcastle remaining virtually steady last week, with Friday's market at A$162.00 a tonne bid and A$168.00 offer.
Sorghum rose by A$5.00 to A$155.00 a tonne bid Newcastle, while barley rose by A$3.00-A$4.00 a tonne to about A$156.00.

Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders said domestic prices held up fairly well in the past week. He saw sorghum rising by about A$2.00 a tonne to the low A$150.00s Newcastle and wheat also up by about A$2.00 to about A$165.00.
There was good money about for any grains that could be moved at present, he said.
The main landmark on Australia's grains market now is the AWB pool price revision scheduled for Monday afternoon.

Closure of the pool by the AWB would normally signal a fall in the market, but with world wheat prices close to the current pool level of A$188.00 a tonne the board could possibly play safe by opening a new pool at A$10.00 a tonne lower. This would cause a cash price fall of about A$5.00 a tonne, he said.
Wheat futures brokers on Friday were undecided about whether the AWB was likely to alter the pool price.
Wheat futures traded quietly during the past week with settlement prices rising about A$5.00 a tonne.
